target_customer: Low income Americans checking SNAP and other benefits eligibility, plus nonprofits, agencies and food banks that deploy screeners; mRelief is a nonprofit funded by grants and partners
problem: Many eligible people never apply for SNAP because eligibility rules and applications are confusing. mRelief screens eligibility by web and text message and helps people apply.
business_model: Nonprofit funded by grants, with paid tiers for organizations that want custom screening tools
product_category: Benefits eligibility screening and application help (civic tech nonprofit)

founders.name: Rose Afriyie
education: University in Pennsylvania (not named in source)
founders.background_notes: TechCrunch March 2016 says she studied public policy and worked with Chi HackNight. It gave her age as 31 at that time, not at founding.

founders.name: Genevieve Nielsen
founders.background_notes: Native of New Orleans per TechCrunch. The founders met at a Chicago coding bootcamp.

technical_complexity.rationale: Rules based eligibility checklists on web and SMS, with the hard parts being encoding program rules across states and getting USDA data published in machine readable form.

defensibility.rationale: The screening logic and state rules are public data, but the SMS channel, agency and food bank partnerships and trust with low income users took years to build.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent was found building the same wedge; states and large nonprofits kept their own tools, and mRelief grew through partnerships.

market_need_then: TechCrunch March 2016 reported 2,000 eligibility checklists in one week, 90% week on week growth, and company data that two thirds of pre-screened eligible users applied and one third received benefits.

identity.voice_and_tone: Plain, helpful, text message first, with a short code 74544 for SNAP

branding.brand_signature: The 74544 text short code for SNAP screening
branding.community_and_virality: Press and civic tech community coverage (Chi Hack Night, Smart Chicago, TechCrunch, National Geographic) but no evidence of consumer virality.

brand_strength.rationale: Recognized in civic tech and food assistance circles through press and partner food banks, with a clear name that signals relief. Evidence is partner and press based, not consumer scale.

outcome_analysis: mRelief started as a Chicago civic tech project in 2014 and joined YC as a nonprofit in 2016. It has stayed independent and grant funded, focusing on SNAP, and an OpenAI Academy write-up claims more than 5.2 million people helped and 2.1 billion dollars in food assistance secured. Growth came from partnerships with agencies and food banks rather than venture capital, so the outcome is mission success by its own measures but not a venture style exit.
notes: mrelief.com fetch was blocked by a rate-limited safety check, so the company site was not read directly. Nonprofit so no equity rounds. Search snippets mention a $15,000 Smart Chicago CivicWorks grant in November 2014 funded by Knight, plus later GitLab Foundation, Walmart Foundation and Google.org support, amounts not verified.
